title: "Nooit meer Auschwitz", the broken-mirror monument (Wertheimpark)
summary: Jan Wolkers laid cracked mirrors on the ground so the sky they reflect can never be whole again. Beneath them is an urn of ashes from Auschwitz-Birkenau. The national Holocaust remembrance ends here every last Sunday of January.

title: 6e Montessorischool Anne Frank
summary: Anne Frank's school from 1934 to 1941, and still a Montessori primary. Lines from her diary have been painted across the front since 1983. In 2001 a headmaster found the old registers and counted the classmates who were murdered too.

title: A.S. Onderwijzerhof, the square the neighbours wanted to call Februaristraat
summary: A small car-free hofje of the 1980s behind the Jewish Museum, built over the metro. The city named it after a chief rabbi; residents hung their own street signs reading Februaristraat, and joked that A.S. Onderwijzer meant 'trainee teacher'.

title: Abraham Asscher's house (Johannes Vermeerstraat 14)
summary: A villa by K.P.C. de Bazel with Egyptian patterns in the brickwork, built for a banker who died before he could move in. The diamond manufacturer Abraham Asscher lived here instead, until he was deported in 1943.

title: Aby Jetomim, the Portuguese boys' orphanage (Plantage Middenlaan 80)
summary: A society founded in 1648 to care for Portuguese-Jewish orphan boys, among the oldest in Amsterdam, moved its orphanage into this house in 1930. Thirteen years later the orphanage's father and mother were murdered in Sobibor.

title: Aldo van Eyck's Mothers' House (Hubertushuis)
summary: A building in every colour for single parents and their children, opened in 1980 by Aldo van Eyck. It stands where the Jewish crèche was, from which children were smuggled into hiding during the war. Now a hotel.

title: Amstelkerk, the temporary wooden church
summary: In 1668 the city put up a wooden preaching barn on the Amstelveld, leaving room for a proper stone church later. The stone church never came, and the wooden one is still here. Vincent van Gogh sat through his uncle's sermons in it.

title: Anne Frank House
summary: The hiding place of Anne Frank and seven others, a museum since 1960. It nearly went under the wrecking ball. Otto Frank himself sold the empty house to a firm that planned to demolish it, and when it was saved he asked that the rooms be left unfurnished.

title: Arti et Amicitiae, the artists' club on the corner of the Spui
summary: Since 1840 Amsterdam's artists have had their own club and exhibition rooms here, from Breitner and the Maris brothers to today. In 1941 it expelled its fifteen Jewish members on German orders, and in 2022 it apologised.

title: Artis
summary: The country's oldest zoo, founded in 1838 as a members' club for the well-off. The winding pond is what is left of a canal that once split the zoo in two, crossed by a ferry, and the last quagga in captivity died here in 1883; nobody noticed the species was gone until 1889.

title: Artists' studio houses in the gaps of the Jewish quarter
summary: After the deportations and the Hunger Winter, the Rapenburgerstraat was full of holes where stripped houses had been pulled down. In 1958 the city filled two of them with homes and double-height studios for artists, an experiment found nowhere else in the old centre.

title: Asscher diamond works, where the Cullinan was cleaved
summary: A turreted factory of 1907 where Joseph Asscher split the largest rough diamond ever found. The streets around were later named after gems. The firm still has offices inside; its gatehouse, fence and nine glass sculptures on the new blocks are the things to find.

title: Asterdorp gatehouse (Atelier Volten)
summary: The last building of Asterdorp, the walled "housing school" where the city put "unfit" families under supervision, later a ghetto for Jewish residents. A sculptor's studio since 1952.

title: Barmat house
summary: Two houses of 1888 merged in 1921–22 by Harry Elte for Julius Barmat, a Jewish businessman whose bribery scandal shook Weimar Germany. His name is still worked into the ironwork of the front door.

title: Beethovenstraat raids and tram stop
summary: A steel plate in the pavement remembers the raids on the Beethovenstraat, a street of German Jewish refugees. From the tram stop here, arrested Jews were taken to the station; since 2025 a threshold marks it.

title: Beth Am, the Jewish people's house on the Amstel (Amstel 107-111)
summary: In the spring of 1923 the top floor of this building near Carré became Beth Am, a Jewish 'people's house' for lectures, clubs and meetings. The Jewish National Fund moved its office here from the Leidseplein the same summer.

title: Beth Haim, the Portuguese Jews' cemetery at Ouderkerk
summary: Since 1614 the Portuguese Jews of Amsterdam have buried their dead in this village on the Amstel, once brought over the water. Its carved marble tombs of the Golden Age have no match on Jewish graves anywhere; Samuel Sarphati lies here beside his wife.

title: Beth Hamidrasj Ets Haim, house of learning with a synagogue at the back
summary: In 1883 a Jewish college of learning moved into this building, with lecture rooms and a library at the front and a square synagogue behind. The front still carries the year 5643 in Arabic and Hebrew numerals; two doors down stands the Jewish infant school of 1862.

title: Betondorp and the Brink
summary: Amsterdam's 'Concrete Village': a 1920s socialist experiment in cheap concrete housing, built round a village green with a library and a community hall but no church and no pub. Gerard Reve and Johan Cruijff grew up here.

title: Binnenveer 11 and its owners
summary: A mid-18th-century bell gable on the Smal Weesp whose register entry reads like a street history, from a woman saddler and a pastry baker to the merchant David Vleeschhouwer and his wife, deported in 1943.

title: Blasiussjoel, Swammerdamstraat 70
summary: Behind this corner shop front, Jews who had fled the Russian pogroms prayed from 1908. It reopened after the war, was famous for its packed Independence Day services, and left in 1967; today it is homes.

title: Blasiusstraat 124, a gap left by looting
summary: A small 1953 shop with flats in a 19th-century street. It fills the gap left by a house whose Jewish residents were deported and murdered, and which was probably then stripped for building materials until it had to come down.

title: Blauwbrug
summary: A showpiece bridge of 1883, built to impress visitors to the Colonial Exhibition, with ship-bow piers, red granite columns and imperial crowns. Critics found it far too pompous for Amsterdam. In Yiddish it is the Bloubrik.

title: Boas diamond factory, once the largest in Europe
summary: In 1879 three Jewish brothers opened a steam-driven diamond factory here with 357 cutting mills, the biggest in Europe. The war ended it; in 1990 diamonds came back, and today you can walk in on a free tour.

title: Bridges with wartime names (Roetersstraat and Plantage Middenlaan)
summary: Walk from the Muiderpoort past the Hollandsche Schouwburg and down the Roetersstraat and you cross five bridges named, between 1982 and 2021, after people who saved lives in the war or survived it. One has hippos and crocodiles carved into its quay walls.

title: Bussenschuthofje (former)
summary: Over a door on the Rapenburgerstraat a gunner in 17th-century dress fires his cannon. The stone named the alley court behind it, where poor Jewish families lived until the slums were cleared around 1930; the gate now leads to apartments.

title: Café Eik en Linde (Plantage Middenlaan 22)
summary: A café named after the oak and the linden of Ovid's tale. It began as a pleasure-garden inn that Artis swallowed (the old inn is now the wolves' house), and its present home was the coffee room of the Hollandsche Schouwburg.

title: Centraal Israëlietisch Ziekenhuis (gone), Jacob Obrechtstraat
summary: Amsterdam's Jewish hospital in Zuid opened in 1916, paid for by hundreds of donors. The occupier emptied it in August 1943; it reopened after the war, closed in 1979 and was pulled down.

title: Centraal Station's two plaques: the cold welcome and the sergeant
summary: In the passage under the station a plaque says in plain words that the Dutch government failed the camp survivors it received here in 1945. In the main hall, a second one remembers a resistance sergeant shot two days after the surrender.

title: Centrale Markthal
summary: Amsterdam's 1934 wholesale market hall, a 70-by-100-metre brick shed with no columns inside, with Hildo Krop's memorial to the Jewish traders the occupier drove from the market.

title: Coöperatiehof
summary: A village green hidden inside a five-sided city block: low houses round an oval lawn, reached only through two gateways. Piet Kramer gave the workers' cooperative that built it a library with a lead-clad clock tower where a church might have stood.

title: De Antifascist (Leo Braat)
summary: A bronze head of an unknown fighter, probably from the Spanish Civil War, that Leo Braat made in 1936. Thirty years later it became the memorial to Willem Kraan, the street paver who helped start the February Strike of 1941.

title: De Bijenkorf on the Dam
summary: The department store that began as a haberdashery on the Nieuwendijk and moved to the Damrak in a wooden stopgap, meaning to go back. Its architect was fired before the building was done. Its hundredth birthday party in 1970 ended in a riot.

title: De Burcht (diamond workers' union building)
summary: The oldest trade union building in the Netherlands looks like an Italian town hall with battlements. Berlage built it in 1899–1900 for the diamond workers, at the same time as his Exchange, in the garden of a theatre.

title: De Dokwerker and the February Strike
summary: Mari Andriessen's docker stands where 427 Jewish men were herded together in February 1941, the raid that set off the February Strike. The sculptor hid Jews himself; his model was a Haarlem carpenter. For the metro the statue was turned to face the synagogue.

title: De IJsbreker, Weesperzijde 23
summary: Named after the icebreaker that kept the Amstel open from 1702, this 1885 café building by the Concertgebouw's architect hosted SDAP socialists, a national chess title match, a billiards temple and, from 1979 to 2005, Amsterdam's pioneering centre for new music.

title: De Kom and the ferry Anne Frank took
summary: Five waterways meet in the basin called De Kom. Until the war a small cable ferry crossed here, the one Anne Frank meant when she wrote in June 1942 that the ferry was the only transport Jews were still allowed. There is still no bridge on that spot.

title: De Mirandabad, the Mediterranean of 1979
summary: Opened in 1932 by the alderman whose election rhyme promised swimming, and later named after him. In 1979 the city rebuilt it as the country's first tropical swim paradise: palms from Spain, a wave pool under a glass dome, and the Jacksons at the opening.

title: De Swarte Mvele and the De Vries van Buuren building (Waterlooplein 3)
summary: A shop in thread and lace opened on the Jodenbreestraat in 1829 and grew into a Jewish textile wholesaler reaching the Waterlooplein. Expanding, it pulled down the corner houses, and their 17th-century windmill stone went to a museum. In 2007 it came back.

title: Deportation threshold, Victorieplein
summary: A threshold at the tram stop on the Victorieplein says that on 20 June 1943 thousands of Jews were deported from this square by municipal tram. The city and the tram company laid it in 2025.

title: Desmet, the theatre of many names (Plantage Middenlaan 4)
summary: Frascati, Rika Hopper, Beatrix, Theater van de Lach, Hortus, Desmet: one building, six names. From autumn 1941 only Jews were allowed in. Today it is a TV and radio studio behind a 1927 front.

title: Diamond Exchange on the Weesperplein (Diamantbeurs)
summary: Built in 1910–1911 to get the diamond trade out of the cafés. It housed Belgian refugees in the First World War, lost two-thirds of its trade in the Second, and burned in 1956 without losing a stone. Now a creative hub with a grand café.

title: Dirk van Nimwegen plaque (February Strike)
summary: A plain plaque in the Borgerstraat for the sanitation worker who, on the evening of 24 February 1941, called on a crowd at the Noordermarkt to stop work. Next morning the February Strike began, a mass protest against the persecution of the Jews.

title: Doe je ogen even dicht, Tugelaweg text monument
summary: A 300-metre poem cut into a pale green steel band along the railway embankment, where K. Michel asks you to close your eyes and see the lively Jewish, socialist Transvaalbuurt of before the war. The letters only appear from an angle.

title: Etty Hillesum's house (Gabriël Metsustraat 6)
summary: A livery stable of 1901 with flats above. In a rented room at no. 6 Etty Hillesum wrote the war diaries that were published 38 years after she was murdered in Auschwitz. The house was saved from demolition in 2020.

title: Fernandes Nuneshuis, a Portuguese-Jewish almshouse
summary: From the late 18th century this canal-belt house gave free rooms to poor Portuguese-Jewish women, above a nursery school. The residents were taken away in January 1943 and the gable stones defaced; one was found intact under cement in 1994.

title: Football clubs' war memorials, Middenmeer
summary: At the gate of an ordinary amateur club, a wall lists more than 260 members of two Amsterdam football clubs murdered in the war, most of them Jewish; 33 names were found and added in 2024. Two smaller stones nearby remember the members of T.O.G. and of BPC.

title: Former cantor's house, Sleutelsteeg
summary: A small house of 1878 in an alley off the Nieuwstraat, built by the synagogue council for the cantor of Weesp's Jewish community. Three Stolpersteine lie at its door for the cantor, his wife and their lodger, forced out in 1942.

title: Former cattle market and abattoir, Cruquiusweg
summary: For almost a century Amsterdam's cows, pigs and sheep were sold and slaughtered here, on reclaimed reed land far from the houses and downwind of the city. The gates, the clock-towered pay office and the chalet-style lodges survive among the business units.

title: Former synagogue, Commelinstraat 16
summary: Under the plain upper floors of an 1880 house sits an Amsterdam School ground floor of yellow and dark brick, with its own door for the women's gallery. It was a small neighbourhood synagogue from 1922 to 1936, and the last surviving synagogue by Jac. S. Baars in Amsterdam.

title: Former synagogue, Nieuwstraat
summary: Weesp's synagogue of 1840, whose Jewish community, says the plaque, was gone by 29 April 1942. After the war it was a garage; since 1997 it is a synagogue again. Stolpersteine lie in the pavement by the plaque.

title: Frederiksplein, where the glass palace stood
summary: Sarphati gave Amsterdam a crystal palace and a square of grand houses to face it. The palace burned in 1929, and the central bank took its place; now its gold vault is open to all, and a snapped bronze tree remembers the banker of the resistance.

title: Friendly Fire manhole covers
summary: Eleven cast-iron manhole covers, and a twelfth added later, mark the streets of Noord where Allied bombs meant for the Fokker works fell in July 1943. The names of the dead run round their rims. A memorial you walk over.

title: Fré Cohen's level-crossing plaques
summary: When the railway through Oost was raised in the 1930s, ending long waits at the barriers, five of the new underpasses got a small bronze plaque of half-open barriers. The first, of 1936, is signed by Fré Cohen. Two later ones were stolen; their outlines remain.

title: Garage West, Bons's birds and Horn's strike mural
summary: The city bus garage got its art late, and the birds by Jan Bons went up lying down although the drawings show them upright. Inside, out of public view, a 17-metre mural by Lex Horn honours the 1941 February Strike, which began with Amsterdam's trams standing still.

title: Geldersekade 105 and the raid of 26 May 1943
summary: On 26 May 1943 a man at his window photographed a raid on the Geldersekade, armed police sealing off the quay and people with luggage waiting in the street. At no. 105 lived Barend and Aaltje Jacobs, murdered at Sobibor that same month.

title: Geldersekade 78, the office of the swindler Barmat
summary: An 18th-century house and warehouse where Julius Barmat ran a trading company in the early 1920s. Within a few years his name was a Nazi slogan, and Hitler used his scandal to stir hatred of Jews.

title: Gerard Dou Synagogue
summary: A small synagogue of 1892 tucked into a row of houses, once called the little diamond shul. The occupier never noticed it. Two weeks after the liberation it held a service again, the only Ashkenazi synagogue in Amsterdam still fit to use.

title: Gerhard Badrian's stone, Rubensstraat 26
summary: A small stone marks where a German-Jewish refugee was shot on 30 June 1944. Gerhard Badrian freed prisoners by walking up to police vans in a spotless SD uniform, and his last hiding place was above a flat of SD men.

title: Gerrit van der Veen College, the school the SD took
summary: "To the Euterpestraat" was a phrase Amsterdam dreaded: from 1940 the German security police worked from this girls' school. RAF Typhoons attacked it in November 1944, and the street lost its name in 1945.

title: Gerzon's fashion works, where a thousand seamstresses sewed
summary: In 1923 the Jewish-owned fashion house Gerzon built its head office between the Singel and the Spuistraat, with three floors of workshops where about a thousand women made clothes. In 1941 a German administrator marched in. It is a hotel now.

title: Goslerhuisje, the last house of the Joden Houttuinen
summary: A crooked lock-keeper's house of 1695 is all that is left of the Joden Houttuinen, a street of the old Jewish quarter pulled down in the late 1960s. It is named after the Jewish metal dealers A. Gosler & Zonen, and is now the café De Sluyswacht.

title: Harry Elte's first synagogue (Nieuwe Kerkstraat 10–14)
summary: Only the front survives: plain brown-red brick of 1913, with a row of windows on the first floor drawn with odd care. Behind it was the women's gallery of a synagogue for 192 men and 26 women. After the war it became a warehouse, then flats.

title: Harry Elte's own house, Stadionweg 44
summary: The architect of the synagogue on the Jacob Obrechtplein built himself a house in 1928–1930 on the road named after his own football stadium. Berlage, his old master, designed the green glass blocks by the door. Elte died in Theresienstadt in 1944.

title: Harry Elte's two Edwardian fronts, Achtergracht 17-19 and 33
summary: Two small 1916 designs by Harry Elte, the architect of Amsterdam's Jewish community, both signed on the front. One is a business building posing as a double house; the other has a foundation stone laid by a thirteen-year-old boy.

title: Herberg Zeeburg, quarantine station and refugee camp
summary: An 18th-century inn on the dike, where an inn stood from about 1675. Its grounds later became the city's quarantine station, whose barracks in 1938–1940 held a camp for Jewish refugees, among them Anne Frank's uncle.

title: Herengracht 598, Samuel Sarphati's house
summary: Next to the corner house on the Amstel, the city improver Samuel Sarphati lived in this seventeenth-century canal house with his wife. In June 1866 thousands lined the canals as his funeral left from here for Ouderkerk.

title: Herman Elte School plaque, Van Ostadestraat
summary: A black stone on a working school in De Pijp remembers the teachers and pupils of the Jewish primary school that filled this building until 1943. Former pupils had it put up in 2012.

title: Het Sieraad
summary: The former Fourth Trade School on its kite-shaped plot at the Postjesweg, almost surrounded by water, with Hildo Krop's sculpture of sea voyages and trades and the motto "zonder moeite niets" (nothing without effort).

title: Hidden synagogue of the Nieuwe Keizersgracht (nos. 33 and 37)
summary: From mid-1944 until liberation the sexton of the Portuguese Synagogue held services in his flat at no. 33, with a ritual bath in a garden cellar. Two doors along, a firm at no. 37 had invented a doorbell you were allowed to ring on the Sabbath.

title: Hirschgebouw, the fashion palace opened for men only
summary: Hirsch & Cie's domed fashion house of 1912, opened to an audience made up entirely of men so they could tell their wives about it. Its top floor held Merkelbach's portrait studio, where Mata Hari sat; since 2012 it has been Apple's first Dutch store.

title: Hollandia-Kattenburg monument
summary: On 11 November 1942 the Germans raided a raincoat factory here and took away its 367 Jewish workers; with their families, 826 people were deported and eight came back. A black column now stands where the factory door was.

title: Hollandsche Schouwburg, from theatre to deportation centre
summary: A theatre of 1892 that the occupier made the assembly point for the deportation of Jews. Tens of thousands were held here for hours, days or weeks. After the war only the front was kept; the auditorium became an open courtyard of remembrance.

title: Hoogstraat, south (nos. 32–62)
summary: The southern half of Weesp's oldest street, with a gable stone dated 1675, a town house clad in sandstone, a little tower house of 1905-1911 and Stolpersteine for the Van Bergen family.

title: Hugo de Vries's house and laboratory
summary: The botanist Hugo de Vries lived at Plantage Parklaan 9 until 1916. Later it was a Jewish youth club and, after the war, offices of the Jewish community. Round the corner stands the laboratory the city built for him.

title: Huis De Pinto, the house that stopped a motorway
summary: A VOC director's house of about 1606, later the home of a Portuguese Jewish banking family. In 1968 the city bought it to pull it down for a four-lane road; squatters and campaigners held on, and in 1972 the council dropped the road by one vote.

title: IJssalon Koco, where the road to the February Strike began
summary: On 19 February 1941 the regulars of an ice-cream parlour run by two German-Jewish refugees met a German police patrol with ammonia gas. One owner was the first person shot by firing squad in the occupied country. A stone by the door tells it.

title: Jac. Baars's own house (Henri Polaklaan 11)
summary: In 1930 the architect Jac. S. Baars gave himself a house that ignores its neighbours: yellow brick, flat canopies after Frank Lloyd Wright, and an outside staircase tiled in black and white.

title: Jan van Eijckstraat 16: where the Wiener Library began
summary: From a ground-floor flat in this street a German refugee spent the 1930s collecting everything the Nazis printed about Jews. The archive got to London in time and became the Wiener Holocaust Library. His wife, left behind here, did not survive.

title: Jekerschool, Margot Frank's school
summary: Margot Frank went to primary school here from 1934 to 1938. In 1941 the two schools in this building were emptied and reopened as Jewish School no. 10 and no. 11; a year later the Jewish Council's finance department moved in.

title: Jewish Museum (Joods Museum), four synagogues in one
summary: Four synagogues of the Ashkenazi community, built between 1671 and 1752, joined into one museum. The oldest is called the Great Synagogue though it is not the biggest, and in the Hunger Winter its galleries were torn out for firewood.

title: Jewish cemetery Diemen, where the Zeeburg graves went
summary: Opened in 1914 when Zeeburg was full, cut in two by a railway viaduct in 1925, then given 28,000 graves moved from Zeeburg. In field U lie some 400 urns from Westerbork, ashes of Jews cremated in the camp against Jewish law.

title: Jewish cemetery Muiderberg, the largest still in use
summary: Amsterdam's Ashkenazi Jews have buried their dead behind this old brick wall since 1642. With about 45,000 graves it is the largest Jewish cemetery still in use in the Netherlands, and its 1948 monument holds the ashes of 28 young men taken in February 1941.

title: Jewish cemetery Zeeburg
summary: From 1714 to 1942 the main burial ground of Amsterdam's Ashkenazi Jews: about 100,000 people under the grass, most of them children, and only a few stones left. Open on Sunday afternoons in season.

title: Jewish girls' orphanage of the Rapenburgerstraat
summary: From 1861 until 1943 Jewish orphan girls grew up behind these two 18th-century fronts. The Hebrew texts in the cornices, naming the charities and the year of the extension, were restored by the residents in 2003, in memory of the girls who were deported and murdered.

title: Jewish memorials of the Transvaalbuurt
summary: A golden Star of David on the Transvaalplein, the playground that became the "market for Jews", Couzijn's relief "Daarom moet ik wenen" and a plaque for the children of the Sparrenweg school.

title: Johan van Hulstbrug and its twin
summary: Two little bridges of 1877 over the Hortus pond. In 2016 the city named the wrong one after Johan van Hulst, who helped save hundreds of Jewish children; in 2018 the name moved to its neighbour, while he was still alive.

title: Joodsche School nr. 1 (Van Alphenschool) and its restored neighbour
summary: In September 1941 the occupiers turned this city school into Jewish School No. 1, for Jewish children and teachers shut out of all other schools. By May 1943 so few pupils were left that it closed. Next door, a 17th-century house was being restored in the same year.

title: Joop Westerweel's plaque, Blauw-Wit sports hall
summary: At the door of a korfball hall hangs a plain marble plaque for Joop Westerweel, the club's honorary chairman, executed in 1944 after smuggling Jewish children into hiding and young Jewish pioneers over the Pyrenees.

title: Kindermonument, the playground that became a market for Jews
summary: First Jewish children were banned from this playground. Then, on 3 November 1941, the occupier made it the market where the Jews of the Rivierenbuurt had to do their shopping. Four bronze children by a woman of the resistance stand at the gate.

title: Kokshofje (Klokkenhofje), Uilenburg (former)
summary: Five small homes in a court on Uilenburg, owned in 1772 by the High German Jewish community. The 1766 Uilenburg synagogue stood in this court; the houses went in the slum clearances, the synagogue survives.

title: Kriterion, the cinema the resistance students built
summary: Students who had smuggled Jewish children into hiding opened a cinema here in November 1945, so students could pay for their studies by working. It is still run by students, in a building taken from a Jewish workers' club.

title: Leendert Pop and Pension Verdooner
summary: A smiling bronze old man with hat and walking stick looks out over the Amstel: Leendert Pop, 83, one of 39 residents of a Jewish care home across the road who were murdered. The people who now live in the house found its past and put him back.

title: Lekstraat synagogue
summary: The last synagogue Amsterdam built before the war: a stone-clad box of 1937, as bare as a modern factory, for a neighbourhood that had grown from 4,000 to 17,000 Jews in ten years. From 1943 it stored the furniture of the deported.

title: Let Me Be Myself (Kobra's Anne Frank)
summary: Brazilian artist Eduardo Kobra painted a 240 m² Anne Frank across the doors of the old welding hall in 2016, in his trademark kaleidoscope colours. In 2017 someone scrawled a protest slogan over it.

title: Liberal synagogue, De Lairessestraat 145
summary: For almost ten years from 1957, Amsterdam's Liberal Jewish congregation prayed upstairs in this ordinary house in Zuid, while it grew under rabbi Jacob Soetendorp into a community of hundreds of families.

title: Lindenbaum's printing works and the boy's first stone (Reguliersdwarsstraat 10)
summary: In September 1912 eleven-year-old Erwin Lindenbaum laid the first stone of his father's new printing works, and it is still in the front. A few years later his father's lawsuit against a rival printer changed Dutch law. Father, mother and son were murdered in 1944.

title: Lippmann, Rosenthal & Co., the bank whose name was stolen
summary: A respectable Jewish private bank of 1859 on the Nieuwe Spiegelstraat. In 1941 the occupiers borrowed its good name for a fake branch on the Sarphatistraat that robbed the Dutch Jews of their money and possessions.

title: Lloyd Hotel and the Lloyd complex
summary: Built for emigrants bound for South America, mostly Jews fleeing Eastern Europe, who were deloused next door before they could check in. Since then a refugee shelter, a wartime and youth prison, artists' studios and a hotel again.

title: Lotty's bench, Apollolaan
summary: In August 1945 Lotty Veffer came back from the camps to find strangers in her home, and spent her first night in Amsterdam on a bench on the Apollolaan, under a horse blanket. In 2017, when she was 96, the bench got her name.

title: Marga Minco's house, Tweede Oosterparkstraat
summary: The author of Het bittere kruid and Een leeg huis lived behind this tall neo-Renaissance gable for 54 years. After her death at 103 it stood empty and stripped, was squatted in 2025, and now faces a developer's plans for a bigger house.

title: Maria Austria's hiding place (Vondelstraat 110)
summary: The photographer Maria Austria hid here from 1943, making passport photos for forged identity papers with Henk Jonker, a resistance man from the population register who later became her husband.

title: Mauritskade 23 and 24, the Jewish Kweekschool
summary: Two schools of 1891 side by side on the Mauritskade. The HBS at no. 23 gave no lessons on Saturday because so many pupils were Jewish; in the war no. 24 housed the Joodse Kweekschool, the Jewish Council's education department and a segregated Jewish HBS.

title: Max Euweplein, a chess square in the yard of a wartime prison
summary: Giant chessmen, a casino and a joke in Latin, on the exercise yard of the remand prison where Anne Frank and her family were held after their arrest. The chess museum of the only Dutch world champion has lived inside the old prison since 1991.

title: Megadlé Jethomim and the Monument Joods Verzet
summary: On the Amstel side of the Stopera, a band of words in the paving traces the Jewish boys' orphanage whose children and three carers were taken to Sobibor in 1943. A little further, a black column honours the Jews who fought the occupier, put up against a prejudice.

title: Memorial to the Jewish musicians, Concertgebouw
summary: In a corridor of the Concertgebouw, seventeen names in gold wire, like branches, remember the Jewish orchestra members dismissed on German orders in 1941. Three of them were murdered.

title: Memorial trees of the Watergraafsmeer
summary: Two trees as war memorials: a prunus with a 1995 plate for all the Jewish families of the neighbourhood deported in 1942 and 1943, and a liberation tree of 1955 in a ring of bricks that read "1945 Vrijheid Blijheid 1955".

title: Memory window, Huizen Kemper, Maasstraat
summary: In the window of a Lutheran community centre in the Rivierenbuurt, 77 names: the Jewish tenants of this church-built housing block who were deported and murdered. A bowl of pebbles stands behind the glass.

title: Merwedeplein, the Frank family's square
summary: A triangle of grass behind the Wolkenkrabber where the Frank family lived from 1933 to 1942; a list of 1941 counts 163 foreign Jews on the square. Their flat at no. 37 is now a refuge for writers who cannot work freely at home; a neighbour ran a secret cabaret.

title: Metis Montessori Lyceum, 43 kinderen and Here Comes The Sun
summary: Amsterdam's third HBS of 1902, still a school. In its courtyard 43 plates name the Jewish pupils who were forced out in the war, only seven of whom survived; on the new wing of 2018 a screen of 4,500 glass lenses throws coloured light.

title: Metz & Co, the New York building and Rietveld's glass room on the roof
summary: Built in 1891 for an American life insurer and still monogrammed NY, this corner became Metz & Co, the country's leading store for modern design, where Rietveld put a glass showroom on the roof in 1933. In 1941 its Jewish owner lost the business.

title: Michelangelostraat 36, hideout of the Hidden Camera
summary: Behind this ordinary front a refugee photographer and a cavalry officer in hiding ran the group that secretly photographed the last winter of the occupation. Their 8,000 pictures fixed the image of the Hunger Winter.

title: Monument for the hidden child and the protector
summary: A bronze man carries a girl's suitcase and holds her in his arm. The memorial is for the Jewish children hidden in the war and for the people who took them in. The sculptor had been a hidden child herself.

title: Monument van Joodse Erkentelijkheid, the thank-you nobody wanted next door
summary: In 1950 Jewish survivors thanked the Amsterdammers who had protected them with this sandstone wall. Contested from the start, it was moved for the metro, then for the Holocaust Namenmonument, refused by residents of a quiet park and stored, until it came home in 2021.

title: Mozes en Aäronkerk, the church named after two houses
summary: This temple-fronted church grew out of a hidden Catholic church in two houses called Moses and Aaron. A relief recalls Franz Liszt, Saint-Saëns and Widor came to play the organ, and in 1975 Moroccan workers went on hunger strike inside.

title: Muiderpoort deportation memorial
summary: A plaque and a bench on the station square. Between 3 October 1942 and 26 May 1944 more than 11,000 Jews were taken from this station to the transit camp Westerbork; most were murdered in the extermination camps.

title: Museumplein 19: from the Reich's envoy to the American consulate
summary: A colonial trader built this villa in 1912 and opened his porcelain to the public three days a week. From 1940 the Reich's representative for Amsterdam, who ordered the Jewish Council into being, had his office here. Since 1945 it is the US consulate.

title: National Holocaust Museum (Nationaal Holocaustmuseum), in the old teacher-training college
summary: The museum fills the former Protestant teacher-training college beside the Jewish crèche. In 1943 children held for deportation were smuggled through the gardens into this building and out of its front door.

title: National Holocaust Names Monument (Holocaust Namenmonument)
summary: Some 102,000 bricks, each with one name, for the Jews from the Netherlands murdered in the Holocaust who have no grave, and some 220 Sinti and Roma. Seen from above, Daniel Libeskind's walls spell the Hebrew for "in memory of".

title: Necofa, an Amsterdam School clothing factory on the Singel
summary: A dark-brick corner block of 1918–1920 that the register itself calls out of tune with the canal. It was built for a Jewish clothing firm that did not survive the war; in 1976 squatters moved in.

title: Nes 118, the cellar in the famous hiding photo
summary: Above a tobacco firm on the Nes, Coen and Ella van Eekeres hid up to thirteen people in their cellar. On 7 May 1945 Cas Oorthuys photographed the cellar; the people they had hidden refused to pose, so the couple in the famous picture are the hosts themselves.

title: Nieuw Uilenburg, Handwerkers Vriendenkring blocks
summary: Leliman's sober blocks of 1917–1922 for a Jewish workers' building fund, home to families from the cleared Uilenburg slums. Its Jewish residents were deported in the war; the HwV monogram is still in the gables.

title: Nieuwe Herengracht 33, the stones of the Portuguese-Jewish old men's home
summary: Over the door, a stone in Hebrew letters and a Dutch rhyme blessing whoever feeds the aged, brought from the first house of the Portuguese-Jewish old men's home. Its residents were deported in February 1943.

title: Nieuwe Keizersgracht 58, head office of the Jewish Council
summary: A double-width canal house that from late 1941 to September 1943 was the head office of the Joodsche Raad, the Jewish Council the occupier forced on the community. People queued here for a stamp that could put off their deportation.

title: Nieuwezijds Voorburgwal 282, where Tina Strobos hid more than a hundred people
summary: A burgomasters' house of about 1725 that became a girls' school, a hiding place, a cabaret and a theatre. In the war Tina Strobos and her mother sheltered more than a hundred people here, never more than five at a time; eight searches found no one.

title: Noorderkerk, where the February strike was called
summary: The Jordaan's own church, a Greek cross by Hendrick de Keyser, has a quieter claim: on the square in front of it, on the evening of 24 February 1941, banned communists called on Amsterdam to strike against the deportation of Jewish men. The city stopped work the next morning.

title: Obrechtsjoel (Raw Aron Schuster Synagogue)
summary: A synagogue of 1928 that owes more to Frank Lloyd Wright than to any older sjoel in town, built when Jewish Amsterdam moved south. Twice there were calls to close it for lack of worshippers; it is now where most Jewish weddings in the city are held.

title: Olieslagerssteeg, the lepers' house, the oil pressers and Maison de Bonneterie
summary: The only alley between the Kalverstraat and the Rokin south of the Spui is named after the oil pressers who sold Haarlem oil here as a cure-all. On its corner stood the city's first leper house; a department store took the chapel's place in 1901.

title: Olympic Stadium
summary: Listed in the nick of time because of its concrete ring of 1937, then restored by taking that ring off. Jan Wils's brick stadium of 1928 is back in its Olympic shape, with a tower whose bowl Amsterdam called the KLM pilots' ashtray.

title: Oudemanhuispoort and its book stalls
summary: A covered passage through a former old people's home, lined since 1757 with little shop cupboards behind wooden shutters. Booksellers have traded from them since 1879; until 1941 most were Jewish, and only two came back after the war.

title: Palacheschool (Lepelkruisstraat)
summary: A city school for poor boys of 1890 became one of Amsterdam's three Jewish primary schools in 1929. By 1943 its classrooms were empty. Squatters later stopped its demolition, and the old name Brugsmaschool can still be made out over the door.

title: Plancius, the choir's clubhouse (Verzetsmuseum)
summary: The Resistance Museum sits in a clubhouse built in 1876 for a Jewish men's choir. The Star of David is still in the pediment. In between, the building was a taxi garage, a horse stable and a police office.

title: Portuguese Jewish hospital (Henri Polaklaan)
summary: A hospital of forty beds, built in 1914–1916 for the Portuguese Jewish community by Harry Elte. In the war its patients, residents and nurses were deported. The architect's name is still cut into the front.

title: Portuguese Synagogue (Esnoga)
summary: Inaugurated in 1675 and still in use. The main hall has no electric light; it is lit by hundreds of candles in the original brass chandeliers. In 2022 restorers found a hidden space at the foot of the Torah ark, holding rolls of 18th-century printed wallpaper.

title: Premsela & Hamburger, the jewellers of the Nieuwe Hoogstraat
summary: A stone over a corner shop still reads Premsela en Hamburger anno 1823. The Jewish firm of jewellers and antique dealers had two shops in this street; the occupier closed it in 1943, and the survivors started again in the emptied shop.

title: Rapenburgersjoel, the synagogue of the 1797 breakaway
summary: A year after Dutch Jews won equal citizenship, a group wanting a modern community left the Ashkenazi congregation, and from 1799 prayed in this house. Under Louis Napoleon the split was undone in 1808. Next door the Jewish seminary trained rabbis until the war.

title: Rechouwous, Molukkenstraat 89 (gone)
summary: A first-floor prayer room in the Indische Buurt, opened in 1925 for some 600 Jewish families in the new district. It ran a Hebrew school and won kosher school meals, but numbers fell; it closed in 1940.

title: Refugee house plaque, Zuideinde 443
summary: On a side wall in old Oostzaan, a bronze plaque says that 30 of the 75 Jewish refugees who came to this area from 1933 to 1939 lived in this one house. Some got away in time; others were murdered.

title: Rembrandthuis (Rembrandt House Museum)
summary: Rembrandt lived and worked here from 1639 until debt drove him out in 1658. The rooms were refurnished from the list of his belongings drawn up for the sale, and one of two pots from his cesspit still holds the primer he spread on his canvases.

title: Saint George and the dragon, Reguliersgracht 34
summary: A white relief of 1945 on a canal house: Saint George kills the dragon, and behind him are twelve faces, for the twelve Jews who hid in this student house for two years without the neighbours noticing.

title: Sarphati's Amstel Hotel and the masseur who saved it
summary: Samuel Sarphati wanted a first-class hotel for Amsterdam and work for the jobless; he died before it opened in 1867. Guests were slow to come until a pioneer of physiotherapy set up practice inside and drew royalty from all over.

title: Sarphati's Amstel end, the grand hotel and the diamond trade
summary: Where the city wall once crossed the Amstel, Sarphati's grand hotel was saved by a masseur, a bridge was rebuilt after the Pont Neuf, a row of houses was saved by swapped measurements, and the diamond trade got out of the cafés into an exchange of its own.

title: Sarphati's bread factory (gone), Nieuwe Weteringstraat
summary: A whole street was laid out on the site of the bread factory Samuel Sarphati set up in 1855. Its steam mill and hot-air ovens baked wheat bread well below the bakers' price, and other bread factories soon followed.

title: Sarphatipark and the Sarphati monument
summary: A park in a hollow, on the spot once pencilled in for Amsterdam's central station. Its little temple to the doctor Samuel Sarphati lost its bust in 1942, when the occupier renamed the park, and got it back in May 1945.

title: Schaduwen, the shadows of the Olympiaplein raid
summary: On 20 June 1943, during the great raid, Jews had to gather on this sports field. A Dutch Nazi photographed them. Since 2022 the shadows of the people in that picture lie in asphalt in the pavement, exactly where they walked.

title: Schaduwkade, the quay that remembers
summary: Along the Nieuwe Keizersgracht, two hundred small name plates lie on the quay edge, each opposite the house across the water where a murdered Jewish resident lived. Residents made it in 2013; since 2025 a line of red balls keeps party boats off.

title: Slijkstraat
summary: Weesp's short shopping street from the Vecht to the Smal Weesp bridge, in the oldest part of town. A bell gable with stone volutes, a gable stone of 1668 and a run of shopfronts from 1885 to 1915.

title: Splendor, the bathhouse of the Jewish island
summary: This 1923 public bathhouse opened Sunday to Friday, not on the Sabbath, for its Jewish neighbours. In the war it was a Jews-only bathhouse and its bath master was arrested for hiding a Jewish couple. Musicians now play in the old bathrooms.

title: St Ignatius Gymnasium, on the site of the Zentralstelle
summary: A 1950s school with concrete arches over its roof stands where the office that organised the deportation of the Dutch Jews worked from a requisitioned school. The old building was destroyed in the air raid of November 1944.

title: Stadion De Meer (gone)
summary: Ajax's home ground from 1934 to 1996, where the Ajax of the European Cups took shape, is now a housing estate. A half-buried ball marks a 'centre spot', bridges carry the names of the 1970s team, and streets are named after stadiums where Ajax won.

title: Stolpersteine for Meijer and Regina Turfkruier
summary: Two brass stones in front of Herenstraat 21, laid in January 2026 for a cigar maker and his wife who lived here and were murdered in Auschwitz in 1942.

title: Synagoge Oost, Linnaeusstraat (gone)
summary: An Amsterdam School synagogue turned at an angle to face Jerusalem stood at this corner from 1928. Wrecked in the war and left empty, it was demolished in 1962; its stained glass went to Israel.

title: Synagogue in a garage, Waalstraat (gone)
summary: In 1926 a congregation in the new Rivierenbuurt fitted out a ground floor meant as a car garage as its synagogue, in flaming red, bright green and soft lilac. A critic found it garish by day and fine by lamplight.

title: Talmud Tora school
summary: The Talmud Tora school of the main Ashkenazi synagogue, opened in 1924, with its name still in Hebrew brick letters on the facade and a tile tableau honouring Queen Wilhelmina's silver jubilee in the hall.

title: The Ancient Order of Foresters' house, Sarphatistraat 8–10
summary: Two 1878 town houses that a British-born friendly society, the Ancient Order of Foresters, bought and merged in 1936 into its Dutch headquarters, behind a front sober enough for an order to recognise itself in. The Foresters left in 1976.

title: The Brilleslijper house (Nieuwe Achtergracht 14)
summary: Six stumbling stones lie at this door. Three are for the parents and brother of Janny and Lien Brilleslijper, resistance sisters who were deported on the same train as the Frank family, survived and buried Anne and Margot at Bergen-Belsen.

title: The Glass Palace of the Joodsche Invalide
summary: In 1937 the Jewish home for the disabled and elderly moved into a modern building of glass and grey tiles, nicknamed the Glass Palace. On 1 March 1943 its 256 residents and staff were taken away; most were murdered at Sobibor.

title: The Golden Bend at war: Goudstikker's lost paintings, a stolen bank name and a secret fund
summary: Behind the grandest canal fronts: the art dealer whose 1,113 works passed to Göring, the Jewish bank whose name the occupiers stole to rob the Jews, the house where the resistance founded a fund in secret, and the church whose sexton was shot in the street.

title: The Jewish schools of the Stadstimmertuin (Joods Lyceum)
summary: Two schools of 1901 face each other on the old city timber yard. From 1941 Jewish children were forced into them: Anne and Margot Frank went to the Joods Lyceum at no. 1. A twisted Star of David over the door marks 1941–1943.

title: The Liberal Jewish synagogue on Jacob Soetendorp's island
summary: A grey block of 2010 on its own spit of land, with a glass cut-out in the shape of a menorah. The congregation's older synagogue was sold and pulled down, and the street named after its rabbi vanished with it. In 2014 the island got his name instead.

title: The Russensjoel and the old "Jodenkerkstraat" (Nieuwe Kerkstraat 149)
summary: Jews fleeing the pogroms who stopped in Amsterdam on the way to America opened a prayer house here in 1889: the Russian sjoel. The street had two more synagogues and a hofje for poor Portuguese Jewish women, and for decades people called it the Jodenkerkstraat.

title: The bookshop where the diary was probably bought
summary: A bookshop since 1931, round the corner from the Franks. Anne's diary very likely came from here, though no document proves it. Its first owner refused to hang the sign banning Jews.

title: The bridge yard and the last of the Jewish nursery school
summary: Behind the fence of a 1920s city works yard stands the house of a nursery school for poor Jewish children that once took 600 pupils and had a royal visit. The school is gone; the house may have to move for a new power station.

title: The city workhouse (Dr. Sarphatihuis)
summary: A vast block of 1779–1782 built to put beggars and vagrants to work. Later it was the city poorhouse, with up to a thousand people inside. Since 1978 it has been a nursing home named after Samuel Sarphati.

title: The city's central kitchen for poor schoolchildren
summary: Built in 1871 as a public school for poor children, this building became in 1917 the city's central kitchen for school meals, with eighteen big cooking pots downstairs and a separate kosher kitchen upstairs. It was fired up again at the end of 1940.

title: The climbing sculpture of the Jewish children's home
summary: A bronze on the De Mirandalaan stood for years in a courtyard with no name, date or maker. It was made for the Jewish children's home that Queen Juliana opened here in 1965, and the children could climb it, and it has been back on its own spot since 2019.

title: The doorposts of the Gerard Terborgstraat
summary: Four empty door frames against a wall, hung with small plates. White for a street, green for a house number, black for a name. They list 169 tenants of one housing cooperative who did not survive the occupation, looked up by their successors.

title: The elms round the Hortus, planted lying down, and an Anne Frank seedling
summary: Behind the Hortus two elms leaned flat over the water for decades. When elm disease killed them in 2014, the city planted their replacements lying down. Their trunks are now curving upwards. A few steps away grows a seedling of Anne Frank's chestnut.

title: The frog stone of Prinsengracht 535
summary: Beside the front door hangs a tiny blue tile with a frog and a Latin line from Ovid: 'though they are under water'. It remembers the people who hid in this house in the war, and their habit of gossiping in hiding.

title: The mirror at the Vondelpark gate (Van Eeghenstraat)
summary: "Sobibor began in the Vondelpark. With a sign: Forbidden for Jews," the King said in 2020. The sign hung on the lamp post at this gate. Since 2021 a mirror hangs there, with a question.

title: The population register attack and the artists' resistance monument
summary: On 27 March 1943 a group of artists and students, dressed as policemen, blew up the city's population register in the old Artis concert hall. Twelve were executed; their names are on the wall. Round the corner lies Kneulman's monument to their leader.

title: The rooster of De Haan's matzo factory (Valkenburgerstraat)
summary: A ceramic rooster, haan in Dutch, once named the matzo bakery of A.I. de Haan, which baked five to six million matzos a year in this street before the war. Saved when the old building came down, it returned to the new block on the site in 2007, inside its entrance.

title: The stumbling threshold at the Artis tram stop (Plantage Middenlaan)
summary: A brass strip in the pavement of the tram stop opposite the Hollandsche Schouwburg says that in 1942 and 1943 tens of thousands of people were deported from here by municipal tram because they were Jewish. The tram company had sent the occupier the bill.

title: The wall in the middle of the school, Weteringschans 263
summary: In the war the occupier built a wall through this school: Jewish pupils at the back, the rest at the front. A plaque of 2005 remembers them, and since 2024 the green behind it has play objects about the children who stood up for each other.

title: Theo Thijssen's school on the paupers' graveyard (Hortusplantsoen)
summary: A double school for about a thousand children, built in the 1890s on a burial ground closed in 1866. The writer Theo Thijssen taught here, and from 1928 no. 2 was a school for deaf children, with Rinus Michels as gym teacher.

title: Theosophical temple on the Tolstraat (Cinétol)
summary: A concrete quarter-circle of 1927 by the architects of the Van Nelle factory, built as a temple for theosophists. It has since been a synagogue, a requisitioned cinema, an art house with all-night screenings, a mosque and a library; now it houses art centre de Appel.

title: Thorbecke, the statue The Hague would not have
summary: The father of the Dutch constitution was meant to stand by the parliament in The Hague, until a minister vetoed it. Amsterdam offered a square, renamed it after him in 1876 and moved Rembrandt partly to make room.

title: Tip Top, the Jewish quarter's theatre (gone)
summary: From 1914 the Jodenbreestraat had its own cinema and variety theatre, where Louis and Heintje Davids played. The occupier closed it, its wood went into stoves in the Hunger Winter, and the ruin came down in 1953. Since March 2026 stained-glass windows mark where its entrance was.

title: Truus Wijsmuller's bust, Bachplein
summary: The woman who got thousands of Jewish children out of the Reich took her own statue home when the hospital it stood at was pulled down. After her death in 1978 the bust was put on the square where, in the war, she met people who needed her.

title: Pathé Tuschinski
summary: A Polish Jewish emigrant who stayed in Rotterdam on his way to America cleared a poor block for this cinema palace in 1921. In 1940 the Germans renamed it Tivoli, which Amsterdammers read as "Tuschinski Is Verkocht Of Liever Ingepikt": sold, or rather pinched.

title: Twelve stumbling stones at one door (Nieuwe Prinsengracht 18)
summary: In front of Nieuwe Prinsengracht 18 lie twelve stumbling stones, for refugees from Germany and Poland, an old couple born in Paris and Oude Pekela, their housekeeper, and a widow who worked for the Jewish Council to keep her children safe. Eight more lie at no. 50.

title: Uilenburg rebuilt, the workers' block and the Witte Olifant school
summary: Uilenburg was the city's first slum clearance. A Jewish workers' association made sure some residents could come back to this new block of 1927; across the street a school served warm kosher meals for 5 cents and in 1941 became Jewish school no. 2.

title: Uilenburg, the Jewish island: the hidden synagogue, the Sabbath bathhouse and two schools
summary: Poor Jews from Eastern Europe made Uilenburg their island. A synagogue of 1766 behind a wall, a bathhouse shut on the Sabbath, the first slum clearance and its kosher school, the school the occupier made Jewish School No. 1, and a head teacher's house that may have to move.

title: Uilenburgersjoel, the synagogue behind the wall
summary: Poor Ashkenazi Jews of Uilenburg prayed upstairs and held their weddings downstairs in this synagogue of 1766, reached only through an alley. After 1943 it stored old building parts for decades; now it hosts a congregation and concerts again.

title: University of Amsterdam names memorial (Oudemanhuispoort)
summary: A steel ring in the Oudemanhuispoort garden, engraved inside with the names of 254 students and 28 staff of the University of Amsterdam who died in the war, most of them murdered because they were Jewish, in the resistance, or both. Unveiled on 30 September 2026.

title: Utrechtsebrug, a sabbath chain and a steam ferry
summary: The first prestressed-concrete bridge over the Amstel was named by newspaper readers and came with a chain to close it symbolically for the sabbath. It replaced a steam ferry fired with coke from the gasworks.

title: Uylenburgh's corner, where Rembrandt lived first
summary: Next door to the Rembrandthuis, on this corner, stood the house of the art dealer Hendrick Uylenburgh, where Rembrandt lodged from 1631 and met his wife Saskia. The building there now was rebuilt in 1889 for a Jewish iron dealer, with the Hebrew year on its front.

title: Valkenburgerstraat 202–210, the street's last old building
summary: The Valkenburgerstraat was a crowded Jewish street of slums and alleys until clearances in the 1920s and the IJ tunnel in the 1960s swept it away. This one housing block of 1877, built for a Jewish owner, is all that is left of the old street.

title: Van Kollem's clothing factory dressed as canal houses
summary: In 1934 a menswear firm built offices, stockrooms and a workshop here, and gave the building the cornice, windows and dormer of the two 18th-century houses next door, to hide what it was. Tile pictures in the basement are said to show the houses it replaced.

title: Villa Protsky (Hobbemastraat 20)
summary: Amsterdam nicknamed this banker's house Villa Protsky, more or less Villa Show-off. Fritz Mannheimer filled it with art bought on his bank's money. He died in 1939, the bank failed and Hitler bought the collection. Half of it is now in the Rijksmuseum across the street.

title: Vlooienburg under the Stopera, the plaque that took thirty years, and Spinoza
summary: The Stopera covers a whole island: Vlooienburg, the cradle of Jewish Amsterdam, emptied by deportation and cleared for the town hall. A plaque for its last residents came only in 2022; Spinoza, born at its edge, has stood outside since 2008.

title: Waag on the Nieuwmarkt, city gate, guild house and first Jewish museum
summary: A 15th-century city gate, one of only two left in Amsterdam, became a weigh house in 1617 and housed the guilds, including the surgeons who hung Rembrandt's Anatomy Lesson here. In 1932 the Jewish Historical Museum opened in its tower room; it stayed until 1987.

title: Washing house and nurses' home of the Jewish hospital
summary: 'In at the Nieuwe Keizersgracht, out at the Nieuwe Kerkstraat', Amsterdammers said before the war. The Jewish hospital between the two streets is gone, but the house at its back door where the dead were washed survives, and so does the nurses' home.

title: Waterlooplein market, from Jewish market to flea market
summary: When two canals were filled in 1882, the city moved the mostly Jewish street traders of the Jodenbreestraat onto the new square. From 1893 it was a daily market, closed on Saturdays. In the war its playground held one of the markets where only Jews could buy and sell.

title: Weduwe met Kind
summary: Weesp's war memorial, a bronze widow holding her child and the empty coat of her dead husband, its sleeves still flapping as if he were running. Since 2018 a steel plate beside it names 79 Weesp war victims.

title: Weesperstraat, the Jewish quarter's high street turned city motorway
summary: The narrow shopping street the Jewish quarter called the Wazepergas was emptied by the deportations, stripped for firewood in the hunger winter and then demolished for a four-lane road. Half a century later the city is still trying to shrink it back.

title: Wertheim & Gompertsz, a bank for American railway shares
summary: One of the first buildings in Amsterdam designed as a bank, put up in 1871 for a firm that administered shares in American railways. Eleven years later another architect doubled it by copying the front.

title: Wertheim fountain (Wertheimpark)
summary: The only park inside the old city got its name and its fountain in 1898, a year after the banker A.C. Wertheim died. From 1942 to 1945 the park had to be called Parktuin again, because Wertheim was a Jew.

title: Where the Maupoleum stood, the "Colosseum", the green glass box and the tunnel
summary: The Maupoleum, called the ugliest building in the Netherlands, came down to cheers in 1994. Its successor was nicknamed the Colosseum before it was finished, the film academy across the square inherited the ugly title, and freerunners train in the car tunnel below.

title: Wild & Hardebeck curtain factory
summary: A concrete curtain factory of 1919–21 with patented coloured-concrete ornaments. Its Jewish owners were deported and never came back; the manager kept the books until the 1970s. Since 1979 homes and three studios, after J. Dibbets and F. Becht bought it.

title: Zitplastiek voor herinnering: Jewish forced labour at the edge of the Bos
summary: Concrete shapes north of the Bosbaan lock look like benches and are not quite benches. Their forms are copied from the bridges that Jewish men from Amsterdam were made to work on here in 1941 and 1942, before many were sent on to camps.

title: Zonnehofje, Valkenburgerstraat (gone)
summary: One of sixteen slum alleys off the Valkenburgerstraat, home to the Jewish poor, despite its sunny name. The city began expropriating it in 1901; foundations turned up in 2016 before new building.
